query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, degradation of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy is governed by selective oxidation of the minor but reactive elements (Al and Ti). These elements diffuse to the surface and at grain boundaries to form a heterogeneous oxide scale (comprising primarily Al2O3, TiO2, and possibly Cr‐oxides) that initially serves as a protective barrier but eventually becomes stressed and spalls, leading to localized microcracking. In contrast, under reducing conditions, the absence of a continuous external oxide layer leads to internal oxidation at susceptible sites. This mechanistic pathway can degrade the fatigue and strength performance of the fcc matrix over time without requiring gross phase transformations that would compromise its initial integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy exhibiting a single-phase fcc microstructure with high strength and fatigue performance and minimal pre-existing oxide coverage.
generation.intervention: Expose sets of identical alloy samples to controlled elevated-temperature conditions (e.g., 1000 °C) for varying durations (e.g., 100–1000 hours) in two different gas environments: one oxidizing (containing O2 or air) and one reducing (e.g., diluted H2 or inert gas with minimal oxygen).
generation.conditions: Temperature in the range of 800–1200 °C, exposure durations from short-term (~100 hours) to long-term (up to 1000 hours); control of gas atmosphere composition to distinctly provide oxidizing versus reducing environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and evolution of a heterogeneous oxide scale at the surface and along grain boundaries, comprising primarily Al2O3 and TiO2, with possible contributions from Cr-oxides.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperature in oxidizing environments, the selective diffusion and oxidation of Al and Ti create a discontinuous, thermally mismatched oxide layer. This layer, initially protective, eventually experiences spallation and microcracking due to stresses induced by differences in thermal expansion and mechanical brittleness. Under reducing conditions, incomplete external oxidation leads instead to internal oxidation localized at high-diffusivity paths, undermining local mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-manufactured baseline, samples aged under oxidizing conditions will initially develop a measurable external oxide layer that, upon continued exposure, exhibits increasing spallation and microcrack formation leading to localized degradation of fatigue and strength. In contrast, samples in reducing atmospheres will show less extensive surface oxide formation but may exhibit signs of internal oxidation. These differences should be observable via microscopy (oxide scale thickness, continuity, and adherence) and correlated mechanical property loss (e.g., reduced fatigue life or hardness).
generation.baseline: Untreated additively manufactured alloy with a chemically homogeneous fcc matrix and minimal oxide content.
generation.boundary: The predicted degradation mechanism becomes significant when the exposure temperature exceeds approximately 800 °C and the duration is long enough (>100 hours) to allow for substantial diffusional oxidation processes. Below these conditions, both oxidation and internal degradation are expected to be minimal.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of oxide scale formation, degree of adhesion, and the interplay between external oxidation and internal oxidation mechanisms are not fully quantified. Additionally, the role of any minor processing-induced heterogeneities on oxidation behavior introduces further uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the as-manufactured alloy and split them into two groups. Expose one group to an oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., air or controlled O2 partial pressure) and the other to a reducing atmosphere (e.g., inert or slightly H2-enriched gas) at 1000 °C for a fixed duration (e.g., 200 hours). After exposure, characterize the surface and cross-sectional microstructures using SEM with EDS mapping and TEM, focusing on oxide scale thickness, continuity, and evidence of spallation or internal oxidation. Simultaneously, perform fatigue and hardness tests on the exposed samples. Use the as-manufactured alloy as a baseline for comparison.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology (SEM, TEM, EDS)
Grain boundary integrity and presence of microcracks
Mechanical properties: fatigue life and hardness measurements
Chemical composition gradients near the surface (EDS mapping)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, after the elevated-temperature exposure, there is no significant difference in oxide scale formation or mechanical degradation between the oxidizing and reducing conditions (i.e., the observed oxide morphology, adhesion quality, and mechanical property changes do not correlate with the proposed selective oxidation and internal oxidation mechanisms), or if degradation is observed without any evidence of selective oxidation or oxide spallation, then the hypothesis is falsified.
